The whole problem on the infrastructure side is that the APIs are slow and you don't have exclusive access. And then you gnash your teeth at people reporting performance problems because of all the defensive checks you put in because all trust has been thrown out. And then you find out that trim() was deprecated and will now be replaced by strim() that handles Unicode a little differently, and you need to port your code before End of Life to stay compliant.

In software engineering, flexibility and abstraction is a benefit: the product must pivot and evolve. In reliability engineering we want dead simple, tried and true. Power is instantaneous. A solar panel doesn't get the same credit for generating electricity when there's already a surplus as it does when that electricity is needed. I don't just mean credit in principle, I mean literal credit. In a functioning market, the marginal value of surplus electricity tends sharply towards zero, potentially becoming negative. Solar generators have almost no marginal cost of production, so there's little reason to expect producers to withhold generation simply because the market price is approaching zero.

Batteries don't just "move existing power around". They can absorb worthless renewable generation that would otherwise have been curtailed, then supply it when the grid would otherwise fall back to coal or gas.

It should also be noted that the remaining solar production doesn't represent the curtailment of emissions-producing generation. It can also represent the curtailment of other zero emissions sources like wind. Probably not to a significant degree, but I'm sure it's not zero.

The gist is that "kinds" allow you to write generic types which themselves take generic types as type parameters.

For a concrete example, suppose that you want to define a data type for JSON objects. You would likely need to choose a type to represent JSON arrays (such as `ArrayList`, in Java), as well as a type to represent JSON objects (such as `HashMap`). However, what if the client wanted to use `TreeMap` instead of `HashMap`?

With "kinds," you would be able to define the JSON data type as something abstract like `JSON<ArrayType, MapType>`, and allow the client to instantiate it as `JSON<ArrayList, HashMap>` or `JSON<ArrayList, TreeMap>`. Unfortunately, in a language such as Java, this is not possible, because `ArrayList`, `HashMap`, and `TreeMap` are themselves generic types, while only non-generic types (such as `Integer`, `String`, or `HashMap<String, Integer>`) can be type parameters. However, in a language with higher-kinded types, such as Scala, this becomes possible.

In these higher-kinded languages, a type such as `Integer` or `HashMap<String, Integer>` would have a "kind" of `*`, while a generic type such as `ArrayList` would have a kind of `* -> *` (meaning: a generic type of one, non-generic type parameter), and `HashMap` and `TreeMap` would both have a "kind" of `* -> * -> *` (meaning: a generic type of two, non-generic type parameters).

C++'s templates permit a similar abstraction to higher-kinded types, and the library nlohmann::json (https://json.nlohmann.me/api/basic_json/) in fact does something very similar to the JSON example that I describe. Namely, it uses `std::vector` as the default for `ArrayType` and `std::map` as the default for `MapType`, but also allows the client to parameterize the underlying container of choice. However, C++ templates need to be fully expanded in order to be typechecked, leading to compile-time error messages that can be long and difficult to read. A "kind" system basically solves this issue by imposing a proper type system onto templates, allowing for more understandable error messages.

You're leaving out some really interesting context there. After the Great Depression the economic equilibrium the world settled into, with the Bretton Woods treaty, is that participating countries, which was most of the non-Soviet aligned world, would agree to base their currency's value on the USD.

That'd obviously give the US an immense amount of power, so in exchange the US would agree to make the USD convertible to gold at a fixed rate by other countries (as opposed to e.g. individuals). So the whole point here is that if the US tried to print a whole bunch of money to exploit our 'exorbitant privilege', countries would be able to take their now devaluing USD and exchange into a gold at a stable rate and make a whole bunch of money. So it was intended to be a self correcting system.

The problem is that the US did print a whole bunch of money anyhow, and when France and other countries said 'hey we'd like to convert our USD to gold' we just said 'nah' and defaulted on our obligations, bringing Bretton Woods to an end in 1971. That signaled the beginning of the modern completely fiat economic system, and led to some wild quotes from the time. For instance the Secretary of the Treasury under Nixon (who was president in 71) has a great quote of, 'The dollar is our currency, but your problem.'

---

Much of math is abstraction (compacting complex ideas into specific symbols or concepts, and then coming up with simple rules to allow their manipulation), and is possible in large part only because of good notation like this. The notation here is really also all first-year introductory notation, and incredibly simple. EDIT: And it is a mistake to imply pseudocode is generally superior or easier to understand, because pseudocode is often too precise, and implies more structure and relations and implementation details than are actually needed or important.
